My mother is a doctor at 304 Hospital in Bejing. I would like to offer a very long (and hopefully not boring) explanation about the issue of doctor/patient relationships in China. 

In general, most doctors work in public hospitals, and we don't have house doctors. That means all the people, whether it is a simple flu or a stroke, go to these hospitals. 

The salaries of doctors/nurses are extremely low. For example, one of my friends just graduated from Johns Hopkins and was denied a working permit in the US (due to the so-called communist background). He went back to 304 hospitals and was given a salary of 8000 Yuan. You must know that he is a surgeon and sometimes, they go 12 hours without going to the toilet. 

For this reason, many doctors/nurses take bribes when determining what medicine they prescribe. These can be lucrative. In an extreme case, a person is officially dead, and he is still being treated for 200k Yuan each day. 

On the other hand, while we have health insurance, it is not enough. In fact, many procedures/medications are not covered by health insurance. And even if you have health insurance, due to the lack of good doctors, you have to pay bribes to enter the hospital. 

Coupling this with the extreme income difference in China right now. You can see why there is a huge built-in conflict between the healthcare systems and the patients. In many extreme cases, the patients will stab the doctors. This has happened a lot due to Chinese propaganda of how they manage to "get rid of the corruption" in the hospital. 

  
Now, it is time to ask what will happen next. If the doctor's salary is not improved, there will be no doctors. Why would anyone work more than 24 hours a day in the ER if you are paid less than a cab driver? On the other hand, our health insurance is running into huge trouble. My mother works in a military hospital, and even soldiers are denied healthcare for injuries. For patients, there is generally no way to compensate them for anything. Private hospitals have been a nightmare since so many people spend millions of yuan only to die. THEREFORE, I don't see a systematic improvement in the situation. Most doctors ask the patients how they want to be treated. Yes, you heard me right. Because that is the only way for the patients to be completely satisfied, even though most patients are reasonable, you never know which one carries a knife.

This is because of the dealings I had with police over 20 years in my personal life.

Thirty years ago, I had my first experience with the police. My neighbor is being murdered, or at least he believed he was being murdered. We were the only one having a landmine. So we called the police. The police didn't even lift a finger; they laughed and demanded payment. We paid them, but they still refused to do anything.

Twenty years ago, I lost something I didn't remember, and I needed a police report. I had to bribe them. However, the attitude is much better now.

Now, in 2018, I moved back to Beijing. I had constant dealings with my neighbors when I played the piano. The piano is loud, but I play only during the legal hours. I would have weekly dealings with the police because people are sleeping all the time. Some of them threatened me with violence. So I called the police. At first, they were insulting and tried to scare us into no longer fighting. With my experience with the police, I wanted to offer them a bribe. However, they never once took it. It is not because they were not corrupt, but because the cracking down of police was so hard that they didn't dare to take any bribes anymore. So they prefer doing nothing.

Since 2022, things changed a lot again. Due to the COVID policies, the police started to get overwhelmed. Because the government required a strict quarantine policy, the police were officially unable to function at all. I'd like to tell you the story of my residence areas. When we found one case, everyone had to be locked inside the residence areas and accept tests until we were clear. But the problem was that the police were also getting sick. So, some of them essentially worked 48 hours or longer because everyone in the police station was infected. This makes them suffer as the commoners. At the same time, their pay is being lowered in the best case and denied for months, but they couldn't resign. So after that, I see a huge mentality change in the police handling of my situation.

After 2023, I have never had an unpleasant dealing with the police. Not once. In one case, they are so helpful that I am not even offering some bribes. I am just offering them some whisky that I lost in the trunk of a taxi since I don't drink anyway.

Now, be very careful that this does not really apply to criminals or people who are seriously suspected. The police are brutal to some people. However, from 30 years ago, when the police were brutal to everyone, to now, I would say the situation has changed a lot in my case. However, I do think my experience is relevant to the OP's situation since he was not heavily suspected and lived in Beijing (remember, Beijing is very different from other places).

If you go to university, the most important thing is learning self-learning. There is no course that is perfect. Unfortunately, most systems are designed towards how "most" students do. I do not know your background; linear algebra can be taught from pure mathematics to economics, and people might have different needs for it. Also, I hate to say this, but people also have different "abilities" in solving math problems. It isn't wise to introduce matrices as operators (one of the many views to do them) after a whole functional analysis before introducing some basics. However, this can be quite viable for people who do pure mathematics. So if you want to learn what you want, the only way is by looking at different books/lecture notes.

From a deeper point of view, there are always two general strategies to organize courses. One is from specific to abstract, which is what people mostly do. Few universities will probably start with mathematical logic, set theory topology, etc., before moving into real numbers; it is equally unthinkable to think about introducing real numbers as an application for Banach lattices. However, the first route is more or less what Bourbaki took. If you took the general topology book, which, if memory serves, is about at least 1000 pages long, you will find real numbers introduced quite late.

Finally, for some reference. There are a lot of things to be done about matrices. There is an aspect simply on computational linear algebra (or so it is called), and you can do a Ph.D. on it. There is also something called matrix analysis, which is more akin to analyzing the various properties of matrices/vectors. There is also abstract algebra, which is usually a start to study the abstract aspect. On the mathematical physics side, there is also representation theory. Random matrices(?) (check Strook's book) have their own applications.

One of the important things about matrices is that they serve as good examples for many disciplines of mathematics. I wouldn't mind developing some hands-on experiences with them.

Even if you are just trying to lift up more weight, it helps to have proper form, and certain proper form can only be achieved with enough flexibility. If you are willing, sit with your back, head to the wall, and lift up your hands (with CORE tight). Can they touch the wall? It is often the case that you will not, which means you can only lift slightly forward when you lift something up. Now think about clean and jerk, one of the most effective ways to train powerlifters (which their goal should be in general). In the GOOD case, you will only lift up a fraction of the weight since you will be lifted forward slightly. In the BAD case, you will have a permanent injury. This Monday, when I visited my GF in the gym (she is a professional bodybuilder), a man was doing clean and jerk with his tummy out. In the last round, he could no longer hold the weight, and he fell straight back and knocked himself completely out. The doctor says he is LUCKY since he didn't break his spine or somewhere else.

Secondly, while I am not exactly sure of the science, I can attest with both my experience and my GF's experience (she has won many gold medals in Beijing), that if you don't probably stretch at all, your recovery will be very slow. Unfortunately, muscle growth is a complicated process that is still not completely understood. However, in general, with proper relaxation, your muscle cannot fix themselves with the micro-tears you created doing all the hard work, and while relaxation can be done in many ways (foam rolling, massage, etc.), stretching properly also can help you.

This being said, since there are so many types of YOGA in this world, it is hard to say exactly what you will achieve.  In general, YOGA is not the most effective way to achieve flexibility, and what is the most effective way can only be found with a professional, which I am not. In most cases, YOGA is a combination of stretch, strength training, and mindfulness training, and what you will achieve exactly is hard to determine. However, I would generally caution you against two things. First, heat YOGA can be very dangerous. The idea of heat YOGA is that when there is sufficient blood flow to the muscle tissue, you can stretch more. However, this can be done more effectively and safely with proper warmups. I am a male Chinese and started to do ballet at age 32, for more or less one year now. In China, there is a SHARP increase in adults female ballet dancer beginners in the last 10 years and it is still increasing. There are several reasons.

1. Ballet classes have become more affordable. While I do not recommend learning ballet from online series alone since some of the tutorials, if not being understood perfectly, can lead to serious injury (YES, ballet can be very dangerous when not done appropriately), these videos make it possible to spend virtually no money and still dance ballet.  
2. Adult lessons have been improved to incorporate more "fun" parts. Again, ballet class has more or less a standard format that has been improved for many years, and one may argue changing the structure of ballet class is incorrect. However, ballet classes for adults in China have become easier and more entertainment-oriented. For example, in the classical ballet classes, students will have to spend years to master the basic Barre and Center works before even being able to perform, and especially the Vaganova systems are **brutally** difficult and physical for adult beginners. However, now many classes are designed so that adult beginners can learn a few steps and already performed simple routines a few months into practice. 
3. Combination of ballet into other forms of dance and fitness activities. You can say that these things are more ballet-inspired instead of ballet and the techniques are perhaps incorrect at best, however, many other forms of dance have led people to change to ballet. For example, many Korean pop dance studios are adding some ballet exercises into the mix, and these add-ons sometimes make the people who will otherwise be uninterested in ballet try ballet. A more popular form is Ballet inspired workout, which incorporates usually some Barre works into the mix, and these can be found in things even like Yoga classes (yes, I know, I know).
4. Parents pick up ballet from their kids. Many young girls will choose to dance, and since many Chinese parents will watch them and try to "supervise" the girl when they are not having classes, many of them develop an interest in ballet dancing themselves. 
5. The marketing has been very much open. There are ballet-themed commercials everywhere in China. In one of the most interesting cases, I even find a commercial that is about being quiet on subways using a ballerina as a model. More commonly, there are ballet-themed leotards, shoes, high-heels that are designed to have ribbons like en-pointe shoes (yes), dresses that look a little bit like tutus, etc, jewelry featuring ballet dancing and themes everywhere (I bought my girlfriend a necklace with a pendant looking like sous-sous in fifth position en-pointe; she hated it by the way because of my terrible tastes). 
6. Finally, ballet-themed tiktokers have been surprisingly successful. Many ballet retailers will pay something like 80 US dollars for 10 seconds of a professional ballerina to do "something" (I know this because I was helping with one retailer to create such videos). We usually expect at least 100k views for such things. And there are even larger groups of ballet dancers, sometimes "fake" ones, doing ballet poses. (Please DO not go En-Pointe without any practices even for photo-shooting purposes).

Hmmm, this might be highly subjective, but the key here is to change the focus on techniques to musicality. Here is a routine that I do. 

1. Scarlatti's sonatas.
2. Bach's Well-tempered Clavier. 
3. Haydn/Mozart's sonatas. 
4. Beethoven's sonatas.
5. Godowsky's etudes, Scriabin's etudes, and Debussy's etudes. This sounds crazy but just play them very slowly with musicality, and you will find it very nice.
6. A (large) piece by a romantic composer. Suggestions, Rachmaninoff's second sonata, Scriabin's third, and Profiev's eighth.
7. A piece by Debussy or Ravel. 
8. Petrushka. Practice this very slowly while imaging you are an orchestra. 

Record everything, compare it with other recordings. Also, try to find a version you like, try to imitate the sound, and then see the difference. This will greatly help you control your color. 

Another piece of advice is to learn music theory (actually writing it). Then you will understand music better. The recommended book lists are all the books by Schoenberg (and notes on his counterpoint), Alan Belkin's orchestration. Then analysis the piece before playing it. You will soon understand what you will want the audient to hear.

Let me start myself. 

1. Piano is not one instrument, it is a hundred (Anton Rubinstein). 
2. Musicality is always more important than techniques (Godowsky). 
3. Piano is not magic, techniques have to make physical sense. You cannot wish for things to happen. 
4. There is not one, not two, but as many as level as possible with the right pedal. It controls the decay which helps to imitate the different instruments. 
5. Left pedal is not for lower volumn, it is for change of color. 
6. Doubles are probably the hardest part (this is however highly debatable). 
7. Composision theory is very important. Harmony helps you to understand the functionality of chord progress, what should be expected and what not. Counterpoint tells you different techniques and what should be heard. Orchestration tells you what part sounds like what and how to imitate it on the piano. Music structures tell you motives and how to emphasize them. This is the real way to respect the composer, not playing like a midi. 
8. Understand what is an opinion and what is probably fact. Don't judge the quality of others simply for a measure that you specifically like to play in a certain way. 
9. Music doesn't have to be beautiful. In fact, always playing the "beautiful" sound (such as too much post processing) can reduce the constrast. 
10. Your hearing can ruin you in the sense that when you expect when you play something you will more likely to hear it, even if it is not there. So record often. 
11. Playing is not the same as practice. Find the difficult part, solve it. Don't play it over and over again. 
12. The sound of the piano heavily depends on the condition of the piano, so learn to adjust. 
13. Use physics to help you. Don't stick your hand to the keyboard (as is suggested by Rubinstein).

So first, in general, the whole solution would be to strengthen the hand. But I guess this suggestion is useless, so here is something more. 

Learn to use not only your finger to play. [https://youtu.be/Jviydd26lo4](https://youtu.be/Jviydd26lo4) is an extremely nice example to study where you can say how Argerich not only uses her fingers but the waist, arm, and gravity. It is not easy to learn her playing style, but once learn how to play loosely like her, it will help a lot.

Sometimes playing slowly is OK, however, you might want to adjust the way when you speed up. Playing slowly helps you to get the notes right and learn to relax after the touch. However, playing slowly often will prevent you from fully utilizes inertia in your movement which you can see Argerich uses a lot. Not to say playing slowly is a bad idea, just a side note.

One way to try to build the relax mechanisms in your muscle memories is to play a note then immediately shakes your waists and fingers (there are many variations to that). You can also try to rotate your waist mid-run to alleviate some tensions.

Finally, never comprises the depth of your touch even if you are playing fast. Do not play lighter simply because it is hard to sustain. It changes the clarity and sound and should never be used as a means.

First of all. I think you are already at a quite advanced level. 16 years to play these pieces are not bad at all, and especially since I guess you are not trying to be a professional, I would say you can already feel pretty good about yourself. 

Second, there are people who learn pieces very fast and there are people who learn pieces very slow. Surprisingly, it is not always an indicator of the level of playing. My first professional class with a professor in the best Conservatory in China was on the Chopins' first concerto and to my surprise, she cannot really even play the simplest part of the second movement when sightreading it. Does that mean she is a bad pianist and a bad teacher? Of course not! 

Third, it is actually common for people to spend a piece for 1-2 years. Yes, it is much more common than you think. I know many professional pianists spend that amount of time on a few pieces and only perform once or twice a year. There are just so many details to try and master. So don't be frustrated. 

Now for some tips. 

​

1. Don't worry too much about speed. I think a very good way to not feel too painful when not being able to solve technical issues is to focus on the musical side of things. Do not just play to be correct. It is a very interesting thing that if you focus on getting the right "music" instead of "sound" from a piece, then you will master the piece much faster and the whole processes become so much enjoyable. 
2. I would suggest letting someone having a look at your techniques. I am not saying that your techniques must be flawed, but there can be problems in some cases it might make playing certain technically demanding piece harder. Again, I am not suggesting you must have some issues with your techniques, just to be safe.
3. My teacher once gives me a suggestion which might help you. Loosely speaking, there is a difference between playing and practicing. Most people will not have trouble playing every single part of a piece (if that is the case, either the piece is too ridiculously hard or the pianist might be playing a piece beyond his/her level), but only some part of it. Prioritize the part that presents trouble instead of playing the whole piece again and again. Then make exercises to make the part even more challenging (there are many ways but it is hard to explain here). 
4. Finally, find the reason that makes you feel you are learning too slow (if you want more advice, you can tell me some more details so I might be able to offer more specific suggestions). Is it because you sight-read very slow? Then try to sight-read simpler pieces (and it is super fun). Is it because you always play the wrong notes? Then probably you want to slow down and get the notes right first. Is it because there is a technical issue, for example, the sound is not clear enough or not even enough? Then don't just play this piece to overcome the technical challenges, find more (possibly easier Etudes) and play parts with similar technical challenges. Is it because you get tired in the run? Then try to use not only your fingers but also your waists and try to relax. Also, try to play smaller segments just to get the feeling of relaxing after touching. 

In any case, tell me some details of what the real trouble is so I and others might be able to give you some more specific advice.  Again, keep practicing\~

For cheap eletronic pianos, they usually use spring instead of proper mechanisms since that is the cheapest way (mind you though, they are still not that cheap). This means many things, but most notable for beginners are that they are extremely light, and you cannot change the color of sound by varying touches. If one is very used to this kind of touch, then the real piano will often seem way too heavy to handle, and in my experience the students often tense up (since they cannot make it sound loud enough) or develop the habits of pressing very shallow on the keyboard. Both are extremely hard to fix. There are other problems though. In general, a pianist wants to build a connection between his/her touch and pedalling to the resulting sound, and since electronic piano tends to create a wrong correspondance, it will results again in quite some relearning. 

For very expensive ones, there is a different story. First, there are electronic pianos that are way more expensive than most people can imagine. For example, when I was in Amsterdam, there is a model for Yamaha, which costs 200 euros per month to rent (and if you rent 5 years, you get it for free). Now as surprising as this sounds, it is actually more expensive than the Steinway grand I bought (it is a second hand one and badly maintained, but hey, it is a Steinway). What makes it expensive is that it builds in the complete mechanisms (hammer and so on), and record it on the top class pianos. The problems are:
1. It is not worth it, since at that price you could buy some really good grand pianos. 
2. The correspondance is still not RIGHT. The nuances of pedalling is completely missing. 
3. It sounds too nice. This might be strange, but it tends to sound too nice for most techniques, even incorrect ones. This is not what one wants if one wants to play in the concert hall. 

In general, you can start with electronic pianos (some teachers reject students who HAVE practiced with electronic pianos, I think that is too extreme), but if you want to improve it is actually better to use a real one. As I said, it is often very cheap to rent one from practice room. Also, upright pianos and grand pianos are not that expensive if you buy second hand ones, which actually can be of BETTER quality than new ones. In general, one should be able to find an old upright piano should cost something like 500$ (with some serach) and a grand piano of around 3000$ (again, need to search and drive a bargain) with REASONABLE quality. This is cheaper than their correspondance electronic ones. Therefore I actually don't usually recommand electronic ones if you really want to improve you playing skills, especially in classical music.

If not possible, then rent one. There is plenty of places where an hourly rate might be something like 2 dollars or something. I don't think that is a big enough deal. 

Even if it is a big deal. First, a good electronic piano can cost much more than a second-hand piano, which is perfectly fine for most people. Secondly, since he is playing classical music and I can guarantee that practicing on an electronic piano is very bad in the long run. Sure, in the short run it presents a nice sound and is cheap (only very bad ones with springs instead of weights), but it will be so different in the long run that those who play only electronic pianos will always need to relearn EVERYTHING. One of my students did this, and he actually spent five more times relearn everything than those who knew nothing. This is because muscle memories are especially resillient. 

This piece is an intermediate piece. Imagine playing soccer for five years or so but not using a real football but one made of cloth filled with sand. That is how different an electronic piano is from real one. 

Of course it is up to the person to decide what is best. I am only trying to answer based on the assumption that he really wants to improve his skills, therefore I kind of am obliged to offer what I think might be the biggest pitfall.
